newsitem.title: USA: Cuba issue democracy, not embargo.
newsitem.headline: Cuba issue democracy, not embargo.

text.p: The United States will keep seeking foreign support for what it views as a drive to bring democracy to Cuba despite its trading partners' anger over the tightening of economic sanctions, an official says.

Undersecretary of Commerce Stuart Eizenstat, assigned by President Bill Clinton to engage other countries in "concrete measures" to advance Cuban democracy, said he plans to start a new phase of his mission despite a wall of opposition to the recently enacted Helms-Burton law.

"We are at least hopefully going to be at a second phase where we can get (U.S. trading partners) to work through their anger and get them to focus at the issue on hand, and that is promote democracy in Cuba," Eizenstat said in a recent interview with Reuters.

He said Washington was not trying to broaden its 34-year-old economic embargo on the island but to suggest steps governments, corporations and private organisations can take to promote democracy there.

Those include stressing human rights, channelling aid through nongovernmental organisations, pushing for social reforms, making sure aid goes to the intended beneficiaries and developing good corporate practices that benefit workers, he said.
Enacted in March, the Helms-Burton law authorised retribution against foreign firms conducting business with property seized from U.S. citizens by President Fidel Castro's government.

Clinton, who would like to be the first Democratic presidential candidate in 20 years to win Florida, where Cuban-Americans are a strong political force, originally opposed the law. But he changed tack and supported it after Cuban fighters shot down two U.S. private aircraft flying off Cuba's coast in February. Two anti-Castro exiles piloting the planes were killed.

In July Clinton suspended for six months a provision allowing U.S. claimants to sue foreign investors who "traffic" in confiscated property in Cuba. But another provision barring from the United States executives of companies conducting business with confiscated property and their families is being enforced.

Many countries are preparing what they call antidote laws and have threatened to challenge the U.S. law in the World Trade Organisation, while Canada and Mexico have considered challenges under the North American Free Trade Agreement.
Eizenstat said he stressed strongly to allies that it would be inappropriate to use NAFTA or the WTO "for what is essentially a political and policy difference and not a traditional trade issue."
The United States would use "every defence" at its disposal, he said.

"It would be a lose-lose proposition," he said of any NAFTA or WTO challenge. "It would weaken the organisations and would reinforce the protectionist elements (in the United States), which already view those organisations as impinging on sovereignty. It would feed into that mindset."

Eizenstat's quest for support for the U.S. position has taken him to Canada, Mexico, Belgium, Ireland, Germany and Britain. On Wednesday at the United Nations in New York, he will meet with a series of Latin American foreign ministers, he said.

In late October, he plans to go to France, the Netherlands and Italy to complete what the first phase of his mission, which he describes as educating allies about the limited nature of the law and allowing them to vent their anger.

Also drawing fire, he acknowledged, is another newly enacted law seeking to limit large investments in Iran and Libya, countries that the United States has accused of supporting international terrorism.
